title: Void Ending in a Square to Uranus
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The square is one of the two worst aspects in the lunar doctrine, an enmity the text grades as moderate because the signs it joins stand two natures apart. The counsel that guards every election runs exactly here: watch the square and the opposition in everything, and keep the Moon from the unfortunate planets in these figures above all.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with a square to Uranus, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his cold, sky-borne surprises. Uranus is nowhere in Picatrix: the planet was found with a telescope in 1781, some seven centuries after the book was written, and no passage of the source speaks of it. What follows is this almanac's extension of Picatrix's doctrine, never the medieval text's own words. Named for the Greek god of the sky, it is read here as a cold, far, sky-colored planet of upheaval, so that a course closing on it ends on a surprise rather than a settled end.
